course.title: Disk Forensics
course.description: A research-grounded, practical course in disk forensics covering evidence handling, forensic acquisition, hashing and verification, partition and filesystem structures, NTFS/FAT/exFAT/ext4 analysis, The Sleuth Kit and Autopsy workflows, deleted-file recovery and carving, timeline correlation, Windows/Linux persistent artifacts, encryption constraints, SSD/TRIM limitations, anti-forensics, complex storage, tool validation, and professional reporting. The course is designed for serious learners who want to move from foundational storage knowledge to reproducible forensic examination of authorized training images. All practical work is framed for controlled, lawful laboratory use.
prerequisites: Basic computer architecture and operating-system concepts
Basic Linux or Windows command-line familiarity
Fundamental understanding of files, directories, storage devices, and permissions
Ability to work in a virtual machine or controlled forensic lab
Awareness that forensic acquisition and examination must be authorized and documented
learningOutcomes: Explain the evidence-preservation principles used in disk forensics and document a defensible chain of custody.
Choose and justify physical, logical, or live acquisition strategies based on scope, volatility, and encryption.
Calculate and interpret SHA-256 integrity digests and maintain a reproducible evidence manifest.
Reconstruct MBR and GPT partition layouts and calculate filesystem offsets accurately.
Analyze NTFS MFT records, timestamps, USN journal evidence, deleted files, and historical sources with appropriate caveats.
Analyze FAT/exFAT and ext4 metadata, allocation, deletion remnants, and journaling at a practical level.
Use The Sleuth Kit and Autopsy to trace files from disk images to filesystem metadata and extracted evidence.
Assess deleted-file and carved-file candidates for completeness, fragmentation, and provenance.
Build normalized timelines from multiple disk artifacts and distinguish observation from interpretation.
Recognize the forensic effects of full-disk encryption, SSD/TRIM, anti-forensics, RAID, and virtual disks.
Validate important forensic-tool results using known-answer tests, independent tools, and low-level inspection.
Produce an evidence-linked forensic report and package derived results with hashes and explicit limitations.

modules.title: Foundations and Forensic Discipline
modules.description: Understand the scope of disk forensics, evidence handling, laboratory controls, and the difference between observations and conclusions.

lessons.title: What Disk Forensics Is and What It Can Answer
lessons.description: Establishes disk forensics as the examination of persistent storage and explains the kinds of questions that can be answered from a forensic image without treating artifacts as self-proving facts.
learningObjectives: define disk forensics and distinguish it from live memory analysis
identify investigative questions that disk evidence can support
separate observations from interpretations and conclusions

notes.text: Evidence as a source of observations

Disk forensics examines persistent storage—physical disks, SSDs, removable media, virtual disks, and forensic images—to recover, interpret, and correlate information relevant to an investigation. A file, timestamp, registry value, journal record, or deleted entry is an observation; its investigative meaning comes from context and corroboration.

items: A disk image is an acquisition artifact, not automatically the original device.
A recovered item may be incomplete or partially overwritten.
Tool output should be validated against the underlying evidence when the result is consequential.

quiz.question: Which is the strongest forensic statement?
options: A filename proves who created a file.
A single timestamp proves the exact human action.
A file-system record is an observation that must be interpreted in context.
A forensic tool output is automatically infallible.
quiz.answer: A file-system record is an observation that must be interpreted in context.
quiz.explanation: Artifacts can support conclusions, but their meaning and limitations must be assessed.

summary: Disk forensics focuses on persistent storage and its structures. Reliable conclusions require context, corroboration, and documented methods.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-86 — Guide to Integrating Forensic Techniques into Incident Response
SWGDE 18-F-001-2.0 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Examinations

lessons.title: Evidence Handling, Scope, and Chain of Custody
lessons.description: Introduces the operational controls that preserve the integrity and defensibility of disk evidence from collection through analysis.
learningObjectives: describe chain-of-custody information that should accompany evidence
explain why scope and legal authority matter before acquisition
document device state, identifiers, transfers, and acquisition actions

notes.text: SWGDE recommends documenting evidence inventory and chain of custody, including a unique identifier, receipt date/time, and transfers. Collection planning should account for device state, encryption, volatile data, safety, and the investigative scope.

items: Establish authority and scope.
Identify and document the source device.
Record its state and connections before changing it.
Control access and transfers.
Document acquisition and verification.
Preserve originals and work from verified copies.

quiz.question: What is a core purpose of chain-of-custody documentation?
options: To record possession and handling of evidence.
quiz.answer: To record possession and handling of evidence.
quiz.explanation: Chain of custody records who received or transferred evidence and when, supporting accountability and traceability.

summary: Scope and documentation are part of technical quality, not administrative decoration. The exact process should follow the organization’s policy and applicable law.

resources.title: SWGDE 18-F-002-2.0 — Best Practices for Digital Evidence Collection
SWGDE 17-F-002-2.1 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Acquisition

lessons.title: Forensic Laboratory and Tooling Fundamentals
lessons.description: Builds a safe lab model using isolated working copies, trusted storage, validated tools, and reproducible command records.
learningObjectives: design a basic disk-forensics lab workflow
explain why analysis should normally occur on verified copies
record tool versions and commands so an examination can be repeated

notes.text: A minimal student lab

items: Use a dedicated analysis VM or workstation.
Keep evidence images on storage with sufficient capacity and access control.
Prefer read-only access to source media and avoid mounting evidence read-write.
Record tool versions, commands, hashes, and case notes.
Use synthetic or legally obtained training images for practice.

notes.text: Never experiment with destructive disk commands on an evidence device. Commands such as disk formatting, partition conversion, or filesystem repair can modify evidence.

# Record the basic environment used for a case
uname -a
python3 --version
sha256sum evidence.E01

practicals.title: Create a forensic work log
practicals.description: Create a small work log that captures the image identifier, hash, analyst environment, and commands used.
steps: Create a case directory outside the evidence image.
Record the evidence filename and SHA-256 digest.
Record the analysis host and tool versions.
Append each important command and its result to the work log.
practicals.solution:
case_id=CASE-TRAINING-001
evidence=image.E01
sha256=<record the verified digest>
analyst_host=<record host identifier>
tools=sha256sum, The Sleuth Kit, Autopsy
practicals.output: The work log contains traceable metadata and does not modify the evidence image.

quiz.question: Why should tool versions be recorded?
options: Because version information helps reproduce and interpret results.
Because versions change the disk image.
Because it is required to recover every deleted file.
quiz.answer: Because version information helps reproduce and interpret results.
quiz.explanation: Tool behavior can vary by version, so recording versions improves reproducibility and auditability.

summary: A controlled lab reduces accidental modification and makes analysis reproducible.

tasks.title: Build a Defensible Case Intake Checklist
tasks.description: Create a checklist for receiving a storage device or forensic image into a controlled examination.
tasks.problemStatement: A lab receives a laptop drive and an accompanying image file. Produce a checklist that prevents uncontrolled handling and captures the minimum technical and custody information before analysis.
objectives: capture evidence identifiers and device state
requirements: A text editor or spreadsheet; your organization’s evidence SOP if available.
tasks.hint: Use the SWGDE collection and acquisition principles as the checklist backbone.
tasks.solutionCode:
Case intake checklist:
1. Confirm authority and scope.
2. Assign unique evidence identifier.
3. Record make/model/serial where available.
4. Record powered-on/off state and connected media.
5. Photograph or otherwise document state according to policy.
6. Record date/time and custodian transfer.
7. Isolate from unintended network access when appropriate.
8. Preserve original and acquire a forensic image using an approved method.
9. Compute and record verification hashes.
10. Record tool versions and acquisition notes.
11. Secure original and working copy separately.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The checklist follows the principle that investigation needs drive acquisition, changes to source data should be minimized, and acquisition should be documented and auditable.

modules.title: Acquisition, Preservation, and Verification
modules.description: Learn acquisition choices, source protection, image formats, and integrity verification before any substantive examination.

lessons.title: Disk Acquisition Strategies: Physical, Logical, and Live
lessons.description: Compares full bitstream acquisition, logical acquisition, and live acquisition, including when encryption or system state can make one approach necessary.
learningObjectives: distinguish physical, logical, and live acquisition
choose an acquisition strategy based on investigative goals and system state
identify limitations introduced by live acquisition

notes.text: SWGDE distinguishes physical acquisition as a bitstream duplicate that can include slack space, logical acquisition as structured files/folders, and live acquisition as acquisition from a running system. Live acquisition can alter timestamps and state, but may be necessary for data that becomes inaccessible after shutdown, such as mounted encrypted data.

items: Physical images provide broad access to disk structures and unallocated areas.
Logical acquisition can be appropriate when full physical acquisition is unnecessary or unavailable.
Live acquisition must document actions because the operating system continues changing state.

quiz.question: Which acquisition is a bitstream duplicate of storage media?
quiz.answer: Physical acquisition
quiz.explanation: SWGDE describes physical acquisition as a bitstream duplicate that can include slack space.

summary: Choose the least-changing method that still answers the investigative question, while preserving access to volatile or decrypted data when necessary.

resources.title: SWGDE 17-F-002-2.1 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Acquisition
SWGDE 18-F-002-2.0 — Best Practices for Digital Evidence Collection

lessons.title: Write Blocking and Source Protection
lessons.description: Explains hardware and software write blockers and why source protection is central to forensic acquisition.
learningObjectives: explain the purpose of a write blocker
distinguish source media from destination media
recognize situations where software or hardware controls may be needed

notes.text: A write blocker is intended to prevent writes to the evidence source while permitting reads. SWGDE states that hardware or software write blockers should be used when possible for physical and logical acquisitions. The exact configuration must be tested and documented.
A normal operating-system read-only mount is not a universal substitute for a validated forensic write-blocking process. Verify the behavior of the platform and tool before relying on it.

quiz.question: What is the primary purpose of write blocking?
options: Prevent the examiner from reading the source.
Prevent unintended writes to the evidence source.
quiz.answer: Prevent unintended writes to the evidence source.
quiz.explanation: Write blocking is intended to allow reading while preventing changes to the source.

summary: Write blocking is a control to reduce source modification; it does not replace validation, documentation, or careful handling.

resources.title: SWGDE 17-F-002-2.1 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Acquisition

lessons.title: Forensic Image Formats: Raw and EWF
lessons.description: Introduces raw images and the Expert Witness Format family, emphasizing portability, metadata, segmentation, and validation rather than vendor lock-in.
learningObjectives: describe raw image characteristics
explain why forensic containers can store metadata and integrity information
recognize EWF segment naming and the role of libewf

notes.text: SWGDE recommends acquiring data in raw format or a well-documented, widely used forensic container. Raw images are flat bitstream files and generally need metadata and integrity information stored separately. EWF can store media images in one or more segment files and can include acquisition metadata and integrity information.

items: Raw images are simple and widely interoperable.
EWF/E01 commonly uses segmented files such as E01, E02, and so on.
Do not infer authenticity from the extension; verify the image and its acquisition records.

practicals.title: Inspect an E01 image without mounting it
practicals.description: Use libewf tooling to inspect metadata and verify an E01 training image.
steps: Install libewf or use a forensic VM where it is already installed.
Run ewfinfo against the first E01 segment.
Record media size, segment information, and available metadata.
Run ewfverify if the image set is complete and the tool supports verification.
practicals.output: ewfinfo reports image metadata and ewfverify performs format-level verification when supported by the image and tool.

quiz.question: Which statement best matches this lesson?
options: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
It replaces evidence handling with guesswork.
quiz.answer: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
quiz.explanation: The correct choice directly reflects the lesson focus.

summary: Image format affects storage, metadata, compression, and interoperability, but does not by itself establish evidentiary validity.

resources.title: SWGDE 17-F-002-2.1 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Acquisition

lessons.title: Hashing and Acquisition Verification
lessons.description: Teaches cryptographic hashing as an integrity check and shows how acquisition and verification hashes should be interpreted.
learningObjectives: calculate SHA-256 for a file
explain what a matching digest demonstrates
distinguish integrity verification from proof of authorship or intent

notes.text: NIST FIPS 180-4 defines secure hash algorithms that produce message digests; a change to the input is expected to produce a different digest with very high probability. In forensic work, hashes can verify that a file or image has not changed between two measurement points.

# Linux
sha256sum evidence.raw

# Windows PowerShell
Get-FileHash .\evidence.raw -Algorithm SHA256

practicals.title: Verify a training image with SHA-256
practicals.description: Compute a SHA-256 digest before and after copying a training image and compare the results.
steps: Compute the source digest with sha256sum or Get-FileHash.
Copy the training image to a separate working location.
Compute the destination digest using the same algorithm.
Record both values and compare them character-for-character.
practicals.solution:
sha256sum evidence.raw
cp evidence.raw working/evidence.raw
sha256sum working/evidence.raw
practicals.output: If the copied file is byte-for-byte identical, the SHA-256 values should match. If they do not, investigate the copy and storage process rather than assuming the image is usable.

quiz.question: Which statement best matches this lesson?
options: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
It replaces evidence handling with guesswork.
quiz.answer: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
quiz.explanation: The correct choice directly reflects the lesson focus.

summary: Hash matching supports integrity claims about the measured bytes. It does not establish who created the bytes or what happened to the underlying system.

resources.title: NIST FIPS 180-4 — Secure Hash Standard

tasks.title: Choose an Acquisition Strategy
tasks.description: Select and justify an acquisition approach for several evidence scenarios.
tasks.problemStatement: For three scenarios—powered-off unencrypted laptop, powered-on BitLocker-protected workstation, and a single folder that is legally in scope—select physical, logical, or live acquisition and justify the choice.
objectives: identify what data each method can miss
requirements: SWGDE acquisition guidance; a text editor.
tasks.hint: For the encrypted live system, consider whether shutdown would remove access to data or keys.
tasks.solutionCode:
Scenario A: Powered-off unencrypted laptop -> Physical acquisition is preferred when authorized because it preserves filesystem and unallocated-space access.
Scenario B: Powered-on BitLocker-protected workstation -> Consider live acquisition/triage first when necessary to preserve access to decrypted data or keys, then acquire according to the case plan.
Scenario C: Single in-scope folder -> Logical acquisition may be sufficient when the scope and investigative question do not require disk-wide artifacts.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The correct method is driven by scope, volatility, encryption, and the evidence required—not by a universal rule that one acquisition type is always best.

tasks.title: Create an Acquisition Verification Record
tasks.description: Produce a machine-readable record for a forensic image acquisition.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a JSON record containing evidence ID, image filename, acquisition type, hash algorithm, hash value placeholder, tool name/version placeholder, source device identifier placeholder, date/time field, and verification status.
objectives: make the record easy to audit
tasks.hint: Do not invent a hash value; use a placeholder that explicitly requires the real measured digest.
tasks.solutionCode:
{
  "evidenceId": "CASE-TRAINING-001-E01",
  "image": "evidence.E01",
  "acquisitionType": "physical",
  "hashAlgorithm": "SHA-256",
  "hash": "<record measured digest>",
  "tool": "<record approved acquisition tool and version>",
  "sourceDevice": "<record device identifier>",
  "acquiredAt": "<record actual timestamp>",
  "verification": "<pass/fail with method>"
}
tasks.solutionExplanation: The record separates measured facts from values that must be supplied by the examiner and avoids fabricating forensic metadata.

modules.title: Disk and File-System Structures
modules.description: Learn how disks are partitioned and how forensic tools locate and interpret file systems and their metadata.

lessons.title: Sectors, LBAs, Partitions, Volumes, and File Systems
lessons.description: Builds the storage-layer mental model needed to move from a physical image to the files and metadata stored within it.
learningObjectives: distinguish physical media, logical blocks, partitions, volumes, and file systems
explain why partition offsets matter during forensic analysis
trace the path from disk image to file-system object

items: Physical storage exposes sectors/logical blocks.
A partitioning scheme describes regions of the disk.
A partition contains or maps to a volume/file system.
The file system organizes files, directories, metadata, and allocation.
Applications create artifacts inside that file-system environment.

notes.text: Forensic tools must correctly identify the partition and file-system offset before interpreting file-system structures. A wrong offset can produce plausible-looking but incorrect results.

quiz.question: Why is a partition offset important?
options: It tells an examiner where file-system structures begin within the image.
It identifies the human who used the computer.
quiz.answer: It tells an examiner where file-system structures begin within the image.
quiz.explanation: Partition metadata locates the regions that contain volumes and file systems.

summary: Understanding layers prevents a common error: treating a file-system offset or partition entry as if it were a file itself.

resources.title: The Sleuth Kit Documentation
Microsoft Learn — Initialize New Disks / GPT and MBR

lessons.title: MBR Partitioning
lessons.description: Explains the legacy Master Boot Record layout and the forensic clues it provides when examining older disks or removable media.
learningObjectives: identify the role of the MBR partition table
explain primary and extended partition concepts at a high level
recognize why partition boundaries are evidence-bearing metadata

notes.text: MBR stores partition information in the first disk sector and historically supports up to four primary partition entries, or combinations involving an extended partition. Microsoft documents MBR as the older partition style. In forensic work, partition type fields and start/length information help locate file systems and detect unusual layouts.
Do not convert an evidence disk between MBR and GPT. Disk conversion can modify the evidence and is a storage-administration operation, not an examination step.

# Example: inspect the first 512 bytes of a training image
xxd -g 1 -l 512 evidence.raw

quiz.question: What does an MBR partition entry primarily help an examiner determine?
options: Where a partition is located and its basic type information.
The exact intent of the user.
quiz.answer: Where a partition is located and its basic type information.
quiz.explanation: Partition metadata helps locate and characterize partitions; it does not directly reveal intent.

summary: MBR analysis is mainly about reconstructing where partitions begin and end and determining whether the layout is consistent with the file systems found there.

resources.title: Microsoft Learn — Initialize New Disks / GPT and MBR
UEFI Specification — GPT Disk Layout

lessons.title: GPT and UEFI-Era Disk Layouts
lessons.description: Covers GPT headers, partition entries, redundancy, GUIDs, and why GPT metadata can be used to validate disk layout.
learningObjectives: identify primary and backup GPT headers
explain the role of CRC32 and partition GUIDs
use a forensic tool to inspect a GPT image without modifying it

notes.text: The UEFI specification describes GPT as using 64-bit logical block addresses, GUIDs for partitions, CRC32 integrity fields, and primary and backup partition metadata. The primary GPT header is at LBA 1 and the backup header is at the last LBA of the device.

items: LBA 0 commonly contains a protective MBR on GPT media.
The backup header provides a second copy for consistency checks.
Unexpected disagreement between primary and backup metadata is a finding to investigate, not automatically proof of tampering.

practicals.title: Inspect a GPT image with Sleuth Kit
practicals.description: Use mmls to identify partitions in a training disk image.
steps: Run mmls on the image.
Record partition start sectors, end sectors, and types reported by the tool.
Select the partition containing the target file system.
Calculate the byte offset as start sector multiplied by the logical sector size when the sector size is known.
practicals.solution:
mmls evidence.raw
# Example offset calculation when sector size is 512 bytes:
python3 - <<'PY'
start_sector = 2048
sector_size = 512
print(start_sector * sector_size)
PY
practicals.output: mmls reports partition-table structures and boundaries. The numeric offset in the Python example is illustrative and must be replaced with the actual partition start from the image.

quiz.question: Which statement best matches this lesson?
options: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
It replaces evidence handling with guesswork.
quiz.answer: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
quiz.explanation: The correct choice directly reflects the lesson focus.

summary: GPT provides structured metadata and redundancy that can help reconstruct and validate the partition layout.

resources.title: UEFI Specification — GPT Disk Layout

lessons.title: File-System Identification and Metadata Layers
lessons.description: Teaches how forensic analysts identify a file system and then reason about its superblocks, allocation structures, metadata records, and data blocks.
learningObjectives: identify a file-system type using forensic tooling
explain the roles of metadata records and data allocation
distinguish allocated, unallocated, slack, and metadata regions

notes.text: The file system is the layer that maps names and directories to metadata and storage locations. Forensic analysis often uses both high-level parsers and low-level views so that a result can be traced back to the structure that produced it.

items: Allocated space is currently associated with active file-system objects.
Unallocated space is not necessarily empty; it can contain remnants of deleted data.
Slack can contain bytes beyond the logical end of a file within an allocated unit.

quiz.question: Which area can retain remnants of deleted data?
quiz.answer: Unallocated space
quiz.explanation: When allocation is released, previous bytes may remain until overwritten or otherwise altered.

summary: A strong examiner can move from a user-visible filename down to its metadata and storage blocks when necessary.

resources.title: The Sleuth Kit Documentation
Autopsy — Digital Forensics Platform

tasks.title: Reconstruct a Partition Layout
tasks.description: Interpret partition metadata from a training image and produce a concise layout table.
tasks.problemStatement: Given the output of mmls or an equivalent forensic partition parser, create a table listing partition number, start sector, end sector, length, type, and calculated byte offset.
objectives: calculate offsets without changing the image
flag unexpected gaps or overlaps for review
requirements: The Sleuth Kit mmls; a training image; Python or a calculator.
tasks.hint: Do not assume every partition begins at a fixed sector. Use the parser output.
tasks.solutionCode:
# Example Python calculation using values read from the tool output
start_sector = 2048
sector_size = 512
byte_offset = start_sector * sector_size
print({"start_sector": start_sector, "byte_offset": byte_offset})
tasks.solutionExplanation: The key skill is translating partition metadata into offsets used by subsequent filesystem analysis while keeping the evidence read-only.

modules.title: Windows NTFS Forensics
modules.description: Develop practical NTFS examination skills using MFT metadata, timestamps, NTFS journals, deleted files, and historical filesystem sources.

lessons.title: NTFS Architecture and the Master File Table
lessons.description: Introduces NTFS records, the MFT, attributes, resident/non-resident data, and the relationship between filenames and metadata.
learningObjectives: explain why the MFT is central to NTFS analysis
distinguish metadata attributes from file content
use NTFS metadata to investigate a file without opening it normally

notes.text: Microsoft’s NTFSInfo documentation describes the Master File Table as a file made of fixed-size records describing files and directories. NTFS stores metadata as attributes; some small values can be resident in an MFT record while larger data may be represented by non-resident run information.

items: $MFT is itself an NTFS metadata file.
A filename is represented by a directory/file-name attribute; timestamps may appear in multiple metadata contexts.
Forensic conclusions should specify which NTFS timestamp or attribute was examined.

quiz.question: What is the MFT?
options: A collection of fixed-size NTFS records describing files and directories.
quiz.answer: A collection of fixed-size NTFS records describing files and directories.
quiz.explanation: Microsoft describes the MFT as fixed-size records that describe the location and metadata of files and directories.

summary: The MFT is a primary source of NTFS metadata and can reveal deleted-file records, names, timestamps, and data-location information.

resources.title: Microsoft Sysinternals NTFSInfo
The Sleuth Kit Documentation

lessons.title: NTFS Timestamps and Interpretation
lessons.description: Explains common NTFS timestamp sources and why timestamp names alone should never be treated as a complete narrative of user behavior.
learningObjectives: identify important NTFS timestamp categories
explain why multiple timestamps can differ
correlate filesystem timestamps with independent artifacts

notes.text: NTFS analysis commonly examines timestamps associated with file metadata and filename records. Differences can arise from normal filesystem behavior, copying, metadata changes, tool interpretation, or system activity. A timestamp should therefore be reported with its source and timezone/representation when relevant.

Do not write conclusions such as “the user opened the file at exactly this time” solely from a single filesystem timestamp. Corroborate with application logs, shell history, event records, or other evidence.

quiz.question: Why should an NTFS timestamp be correlated with other artifacts?
options: Because timestamps can have multiple meanings and can be changed by normal system activity.
quiz.answer: Because timestamps can have multiple meanings and can be changed by normal system activity.
quiz.explanation: Correlation reduces the risk of over-interpreting a single metadata field.

summary: Timestamps are useful temporal evidence only when their semantics, source, timezone, and limitations are understood.

resources.title: Microsoft Sysinternals NTFSInfo
SWGDE 18-F-001-2.0 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Examinations

lessons.title: USN Journal, Alternate Data Streams, and NTFS-Specific Evidence
lessons.description: Explores NTFS-specific artifacts that can add file activity context or reveal data that is not obvious from the primary filename alone.
learningObjectives: describe the purpose of the NTFS USN Change Journal at a high level
explain alternate data streams and their forensic relevance
identify limitations such as journal rollover and artifact availability

notes.text: The NTFS USN Change Journal records changes to files and directories for filesystem management. Forensic tools can parse it to identify events such as file creation, deletion, rename, and data changes when records are available. Alternate Data Streams (ADS) allow additional named data streams associated with an NTFS file; they can be legitimate but are also worth examining when an investigation calls for hidden or non-obvious content.

items: A journal is not an immutable audit log. Records can roll over and can be absent.
A USN event shows a filesystem change, not necessarily the human reason for the change.
ADS analysis should distinguish normal application behavior from suspicious use.

quiz.question: What does a USN journal record primarily represent?
options: A cryptographic private key by definition
quiz.answer: Filesystem change information
quiz.explanation: The USN Change Journal is a filesystem change-tracking mechanism.

summary: NTFS journals and ADS can enrich an examination, but they must be interpreted as filesystem artifacts with retention and semantic limits.

resources.title: Microsoft Sysinternals NTFSInfo
The Sleuth Kit Documentation

lessons.title: Windows Recycle Bin and Volume Shadow Copies
lessons.description: Introduces two Windows evidence sources that can preserve context about deleted files or historical filesystem states.
learningObjectives: explain the purpose of the Windows Recycle Bin
describe how Volume Shadow Copies can provide historical views
avoid treating recovered historical copies as proof of a specific user action

notes.text: The Windows Recycle Bin can preserve deleted user files together with metadata used by Windows to manage the item. Volume Shadow Copy Service (VSS) snapshots can preserve earlier filesystem states when snapshots exist and are accessible. These sources can be valuable for recovery and temporal comparison.

items: Recycle Bin records and naming vary by Windows version and user context.
VSS availability depends on system configuration and snapshot retention.
Historical copies should be compared with the live filesystem to identify what changed.

practicals.title: Compare current and historical file presence
practicals.description: Using an authorized training image with a VSS-capable dataset, compare a target file across the current filesystem and a historical snapshot.
steps: Locate the target path in the current filesystem.
Locate the same path or file in an available snapshot.
Record differences in existence, size, timestamps, and content hash.
State which observations are directly supported and which require interpretation.
practicals.solution: Document the comparison in a table: current state, historical state, hashes, timestamps, and examiner interpretation. Do not alter the evidence snapshot.
practicals.output: The result is a documented comparison that can show that a file existed or differed at an earlier point when the snapshot actually contains it.

quiz.question: Which statement best matches this lesson?
options: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
It replaces evidence handling with guesswork.
quiz.answer: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
quiz.explanation: The correct choice directly reflects the lesson focus.

summary: Deleted-file analysis benefits from checking both current metadata and available historical sources such as Recycle Bin content and VSS snapshots.

tasks.title: Correlate an NTFS File Record
tasks.description: Build a short forensic finding from an NTFS file record and two corroborating artifacts.
tasks.problemStatement: Given a file’s MFT metadata and two independent artifact observations, write a finding that separates facts, interpretation, and uncertainty.
requirements: A training NTFS image or pre-collected artifact output.
tasks.hint: Use a three-part structure: Observed, Correlated, Conclusion/Limitations.
tasks.solutionCode:
Observed: NTFS metadata shows the target path, size, and recorded timestamp values.
Correlated: A separate artifact records activity involving the same path or content near the relevant time.
Conclusion: The evidence supports that the file existed and was involved in the recorded activity; it does not by itself establish the human actor or intent.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution models evidence-based wording and avoids turning filesystem metadata into unsupported claims about a person.

modules.title: FAT, exFAT, and ext4 Analysis
modules.description: Understand common non-NTFS disk filesystems and the structures that support deleted-file recovery and low-level validation.

lessons.title: FAT File Systems and Deleted Directory Entries
lessons.description: Introduces FAT allocation tables, directory entries, short/long names, cluster chains, and the forensic meaning of deleted entries.
learningObjectives: explain the role of the FAT allocation table
describe how directory entries relate to file allocation
identify why deleted-file recovery can be partial

notes.text: FAT-family file systems use allocation structures and directory entries to map filenames to clusters. When a file is deleted, directory metadata and allocation information can change while portions of content remain until reused. Recovery depends on how much metadata survives and whether clusters have been overwritten.
A deleted filename or recovered cluster sequence is not enough to guarantee that a file is complete. Validate size, allocation, signatures, content consistency, and neighboring metadata.

quiz.question: What most threatens recovery of a deleted FAT file?
options: Subsequent reuse or overwrite of its clusters
quiz.answer: Subsequent reuse or overwrite of its clusters
quiz.explanation: Once old clusters are reused, previous file content can be destroyed or mixed with newer data.

summary: FAT recovery is a reconstruction problem: the examiner must determine which metadata and clusters still belong together.

resources.title: The Sleuth Kit Documentation

lessons.title: exFAT and Removable-Media Considerations
lessons.description: Covers exFAT as a modern removable-media filesystem and highlights why removable media deserves careful acquisition and contextual analysis.
learningObjectives: recognize exFAT as a filesystem used on removable/storage media
identify why allocation metadata and directory records matter
plan examination around device context and acquisition provenance

notes.text: exFAT is designed for large removable and flash-oriented storage. In forensics, the same broad principles apply: preserve the source, identify filesystem structures, parse metadata, recover deleted content where possible, and correlate timestamps and device context. The examiner should verify parser support and version-specific behavior rather than assuming FAT32 and exFAT are identical.

items: Record the source device and acquisition method because removable media can move between systems.
Consider filesystem metadata together with host artifacts when the investigation concerns how the media was used.

quiz.question: Why is host correlation useful for removable-media cases?
options: The same media may have been connected to multiple systems.
It eliminates the need for hashing.
quiz.answer: The same media may have been connected to multiple systems.
quiz.explanation: Host artifacts can help establish when and where a removable device was observed or used, subject to artifact availability and interpretation.

summary: Removable-media forensics combines filesystem analysis with provenance and host correlation.

lessons.title: ext4 Superblock, Inodes, and Allocation
lessons.description: Introduces the ext4 structures that explain how Linux files are represented and located on disk.
learningObjectives: describe the roles of the ext4 superblock and inodes
explain how allocation metadata points toward file data
identify why low-level ext4 knowledge improves forensic validation

notes.text: ext4 uses a superblock for filesystem-wide information and inodes for file metadata and block mapping. The filesystem also uses block groups and allocation structures. Understanding these layers helps an examiner validate parser output and reason about deleted or damaged metadata.

items: An inode is metadata for a filesystem object; filenames are associated through directory entries.
The superblock contains filesystem parameters needed to interpret structures.
Parser results should be checked against the image when an important finding depends on a low-level field.

quiz.question: Which ext4 structure primarily stores metadata for a file object?
quiz.answer: Inode
quiz.explanation: ext4 uses inodes to store metadata and block mapping information for filesystem objects.

summary: ext4 analysis requires understanding the difference between inode metadata, directory names, and allocated data blocks.

resources.title: Linux Kernel Documentation — ext4 journal
The Sleuth Kit Documentation

lessons.title: ext4 Journaling and Crash-Recovery Evidence
lessons.description: Explains the jbd2 journal and why journal contents can provide historical filesystem metadata while still having strict limits.
learningObjectives: explain the purpose of ext4 journaling
distinguish metadata journaling from guaranteed file-content history
recognize journal transactions and commit records at a high level

notes.text: Linux kernel documentation states that ext4 commonly journals filesystem metadata and uses jbd2 for journaling. In the default data=ordered mode, metadata is journaled but file data blocks are not guaranteed to be in a crash-consistent state. Journal transactions use descriptor and commit structures, and incomplete or invalid transactions can be discarded during replay.
A journal is not a complete chronological recording of every user action. Retention, filesystem mode, crashes, and subsequent reuse limit what can be inferred.

practicals.title: Inspect ext4 metadata in a lab image
practicals.description: Use Sleuth Kit or an equivalent parser to identify ext4 metadata and relate an inode to a filename.
steps: Identify the ext4 filesystem in the image.
Use the filesystem listing tool to locate a target file.
Record the file’s inode number and metadata.
Explain how the directory entry links the name to the inode.
practicals.output: The tools show the directory/file metadata and inode details. Replace the placeholders with values from the actual training image and mmls output.

quiz.question: Which statement best matches this lesson?
options: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
It replaces evidence handling with guesswork.
quiz.answer: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
quiz.explanation: The correct choice directly reflects the lesson focus.

summary: ext4 journaling can preserve useful filesystem-state information, but it should be interpreted as filesystem recovery metadata rather than a user activity log.

tasks.title: Recover and Validate a Deleted-File Candidate
tasks.description: Assess whether a deleted-file candidate is complete and attributable to a particular filesystem location.
tasks.problemStatement: Given a recovered file candidate, determine whether its metadata, size, cluster/block continuity, and content are internally consistent.
objectives: distinguish recovered evidence from reconstructed inference
requirements: A synthetic or authorized forensic image containing a deleted-file scenario; Sleuth Kit or equivalent.
tasks.hint: Check metadata first, then allocation continuity, then content consistency and hash the recovered output.
tasks.solutionCode:
# Example validation workflow
fls -r -d -o <offset> evidence.raw
# Inspect a candidate inode/file record
istat -o <offset> evidence.raw <inode>
# Extract only after documenting the source record
icat -o <offset> evidence.raw <inode> > recovered.bin
sha256sum recovered.bin
tasks.solutionExplanation: A defensible recovery records where the candidate came from, what metadata survived, whether the data is contiguous/consistent, and the digest of the extracted copy.

modules.title: Forensic Analysis Tools and Workflows
modules.description: Build repeatable workflows with The Sleuth Kit, Autopsy, read-only examination methods, and low-level validation tools.

lessons.title: The Sleuth Kit Core Workflow
lessons.description: Teaches a command-line workflow for partition discovery, filesystem listing, metadata inspection, and file extraction.
learningObjectives: use mmls to inspect partition structures
use fls and istat to locate and inspect filesystem objects
use icat to extract a file object from an image

notes.text:
# Partition layout
mmls evidence.raw

# List files recursively using a partition offset reported by mmls
fls -r -o <offset-sectors> evidence.raw

# Inspect metadata for an inode/file entry
istat -o <offset-sectors> evidence.raw <inode>

# Extract an inode to a separate working file
icat -o <offset-sectors> evidence.raw <inode> > extracted.bin

practicals.title: Trace a file from partition to extracted bytes
practicals.description: Perform a complete TSK trace on a training image.
steps: Run mmls and select the target partition.
Run fls to identify a target path and inode/metadata address.
Run istat on that object.
Use icat to extract the object to the case working directory.
Hash the extracted file and record the source object identifier.
practicals.solution: Use the four-tool sequence mmls → fls → istat → icat, substituting the actual offset and inode from the image.
practicals.output: The student produces a reproducible chain from disk layout to filesystem metadata to extracted bytes.

quiz.question: Which statement best matches this lesson?
options: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
It replaces evidence handling with guesswork.
quiz.answer: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
quiz.explanation: The correct choice directly reflects the lesson focus.

summary: The Sleuth Kit separates image/partition interpretation from filesystem object analysis, making the workflow transparent and scriptable.

lessons.title: Autopsy Case Creation and Ingest
lessons.description: Introduces Autopsy as a graphical forensic platform built around The Sleuth Kit and explains the case/data-source/ingest model.
learningObjectives: create a forensic case in Autopsy
add a disk image as a data source
explain what ingest modules do and why module selection matters

notes.text: Autopsy is a digital forensics platform and graphical interface to The Sleuth Kit and other forensic tools. Its ingest framework analyzes data sources and files; examples include hash calculation, file-type identification, and artifact analysis. The examiner should choose modules based on the investigative question and validate important findings independently when appropriate.

items: A case is the organizational boundary for evidence and results.
Ingest can be computationally expensive; enable only useful modules for the exercise.
Tag or export findings with enough context to reproduce how they were obtained.

quiz.question: What is an Autopsy ingest module used for?
options: Analyzing a data source or its files and producing forensic results.
quiz.answer: Analyzing a data source or its files and producing forensic results.
quiz.explanation: Autopsy ingest modules perform analysis over added data sources and files.

summary: Autopsy accelerates examination but does not remove the examiner’s responsibility to understand the underlying artifacts.

lessons.title: Read-Only Mounting and Controlled Examination
lessons.description: Shows how mounting a filesystem can expose evidence to normal tools while introducing modification risk, and presents safer alternatives for examination.
learningObjectives: explain why normal mounting can modify metadata
use Linux loop-device read-only options in a lab
verify that an analysis mount is not intended for writing

notes.text: Mounting a filesystem through an ordinary operating-system path can trigger metadata updates or other writes. For a forensic workflow, use a validated read-only method or a forensic tool that parses the image without mounting it. If a lab requires mounting, document the exact options and confirm the operating system behavior.

# Example lab-only read-only mount pattern; verify device/image handling first
mkdir -p /mnt/forensic
sudo mount -o ro,loop,show_sys_files evidence.raw /mnt/forensic
# After examination
sudo umount /mnt/forensic

quiz.question: Why is a forensic parser often preferable to normal mounting?
options: It can interpret the image without exposing it to normal filesystem write behavior.
quiz.answer: It can interpret the image without exposing it to normal filesystem write behavior.
quiz.explanation: Parsing an image directly can avoid filesystem writes associated with ordinary mounting, while still requiring tool validation.

summary: Read-only mounting reduces write risk but must be treated as a controlled technique rather than an assumption.

lessons.title: File Signatures, Strings, and Hex-Level Validation
lessons.description: Teaches low-level inspection methods that help validate file types and recover context when filenames or filesystem metadata are misleading.
learningObjectives: distinguish filename extension from file signature
use file and strings on extracted evidence copies
use a hex viewer or xxd to inspect bytes without editing them

notes.text: A filename extension is a naming convention, while a file signature or magic value is evidence about the byte structure at the beginning of a file. Strings extraction can reveal readable fragments but is not proof that the strings are meaningful or complete. Hex inspection is useful when validating parser output or inspecting a suspicious header.

file extracted.bin
strings -a -n 8 extracted.bin | head -n 40
xxd -g 1 -l 64 extracted.bin

quiz.question: Why can a file extension be misleading?
options: Extensions can be renamed without changing the underlying bytes.
Extensions are stored only in RAM.
quiz.answer: Extensions can be renamed without changing the underlying bytes.
quiz.explanation: A user or application can rename a file while leaving its content unchanged.

summary: Low-level views are validation tools: they can confirm or challenge higher-level interpretations without changing the evidence copy.

tasks.title: Build a Reproducible TSK Examination Script
tasks.description: Write a shell script that records the partition table and a recursive file listing for a supplied image.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a script that accepts an image path and writes mmls and fls output into a case directory without modifying the image.
objectives: separate evidence path from output path
requirements: Linux shell; The Sleuth Kit installed; a training image.
tasks.hint: Use set -euo pipefail and never redirect output back into the evidence path.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The script keeps evidence read-only, records execution context, and writes results to a separate directory. The OFFSET value must be selected from the actual partition layout rather than assumed.

modules.title: Recovery, Carving, Timelines, and Artifact Correlation
modules.description: Recover deleted or partially referenced data, construct timelines, and correlate filesystem artifacts with operating-system and application evidence.

lessons.title: Deleted Files, Unallocated Space, and Slack
lessons.description: Explains what deletion changes and how examiners distinguish metadata remnants, unallocated content, and slack-space artifacts.
learningObjectives: define unallocated space and file slack
explain why deleted content may survive
assess whether a recovered file is complete or fragmented

notes.text: Deletion normally removes or changes filesystem references to a file rather than instantly erasing every byte. Recovery is possible when metadata and/or content remain and have not been overwritten. Slack space is the area between a file’s logical end and the end of its allocated storage unit and can contain residual bytes.

items: Recovery success depends on filesystem, allocation reuse, fragmentation, TRIM behavior, and acquisition timing.
Recovered fragments can belong to different historical files if blocks were reused.
Hashing a recovered file proves the integrity of the extracted copy, not its historical completeness.

quiz.question: What is a major limitation of deleted-file recovery?
options: Previous data may have been overwritten or fragmented.
All deleted files remain perfectly intact.
Partition tables always preserve file contents.
quiz.answer: Previous data may have been overwritten or fragmented.
quiz.explanation: Filesystem reuse can destroy or fragment remnants needed for recovery.

summary: Deleted-file recovery is reconstruction under uncertainty, not a guaranteed “undelete” operation.

resources.title: The Sleuth Kit Documentation
SWGDE 18-F-001-2.0 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Examinations

lessons.title: File Carving and Fragmentation
lessons.description: Introduces carving from raw data using file signatures and structural validation, including why carving can produce false positives and incomplete files.
learningObjectives: explain signature-based carving
identify common causes of false positives
validate carved files using internal structure and context

notes.text: File carving searches data outside normal filesystem allocation metadata for recognizable file structures. A carved object can be useful when directory metadata is missing, but carving can misidentify random bytes as headers and can fail on fragmented files. The examiner should validate file structure, size, internal consistency, and surrounding context.
Never treat a carved file’s existence as proof that the original filesystem contained that exact complete file at a particular time unless corroborating evidence supports that conclusion.

quiz.question: Why can carving produce false positives?
options: Random data can contain byte sequences resembling file signatures.
Carving requires a valid MFT entry for every result.
Carving automatically knows the original filename.
quiz.answer: Random data can contain byte sequences resembling file signatures.
quiz.explanation: Signature matching alone cannot establish that a byte sequence is a valid complete file.

summary: Carving is a recovery technique of last resort or complement, and validation is essential because metadata relationships are absent or weakened.

resources.title: The Sleuth Kit Documentation

lessons.title: Timeline Analysis and Timestamp Normalization
lessons.description: Teaches event timelines as a correlation tool and explains normalization, time zones, clock skew, and the difference between filesystem and application events.
learningObjectives: construct a timeline from multiple artifact sources
normalize timestamps to a documented timezone
identify clock and artifact limitations

notes.text: A forensic timeline combines events from different sources—filesystem metadata, journals, operating-system logs, application databases, and other artifacts—to create a temporal view. Before correlating events, document the timezone and timestamp representation. Clock drift, daylight-saving changes, copying, virtualization, and parser interpretation can affect the apparent order.

items: Preserve the original timestamp value and source.
Normalize into a common representation for comparison.
Keep source and timezone metadata beside the normalized value.
Correlate independent event types.
State uncertainty when ordering is not reliable.

practicals.title: Build a small evidence timeline
practicals.description: Create a CSV timeline from three artifact sources supplied in a training case.
steps: Create columns: timestamp_utc, source, artifact, observation, confidence.
Convert all supplied times to UTC without deleting the original source value from notes.
Sort by timestamp.
Identify two correlations and one uncertainty.
practicals.solution:
timestamp_utc,source,artifact,observation,confidence
2026-01-10T09:00:00Z,filesystem,NTFS metadata,target file record observed,medium
2026-01-10T09:02:00Z,application,SQLite record,target item referenced,medium
2026-01-10T09:04:00Z,system,event log,related process event,medium
practicals.output: The CSV is a normalized analytical view. The sample timestamps are training data for the exercise and are not evidence of a real case.

options: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
It replaces evidence handling with guesswork.
quiz.answer: It concerns the disk-forensics concept taught here.
quiz.explanation: The correct choice directly reflects the lesson focus.

summary: Timeline analysis is strongest when events from independent sources converge on the same hypothesis.

lessons.title: Windows User and Application Artifacts on Disk
lessons.description: Shows how disk forensics extends beyond raw files into registry hives, application databases, browser artifacts, and other persistent traces.
learningObjectives: explain what Windows registry hives contain at a high level
identify why application artifacts can corroborate filesystem evidence
separate artifact presence from claims about user intent

notes.text: Microsoft describes registry hives as logical groups of keys, subkeys, and values backed by files loaded into memory. User profile hives contain information about application settings, desktop, environment, network connections, and printers. Other disk artifacts such as browser databases, shortcut records, application caches, and event logs can provide context when available.

items: Artifact paths and formats vary by operating-system and application version.
Use a parser appropriate to the artifact and preserve the source database/hive for validation.
Corroboration is more reliable than treating one application artifact as a complete activity history.

quiz.question: What is a Windows registry hive?
options: A logical group of registry keys, subkeys, and values backed by supporting files.
quiz.answer: A logical group of registry keys, subkeys, and values backed by supporting files.
quiz.explanation: Microsoft documents registry hives as logical groups backed by supporting files.

summary: Disk forensics can reconstruct user and application context from persistent artifacts, but artifact semantics and retention must be understood.

tasks.title: Produce a Correlated Timeline Finding
tasks.description: Create a concise finding from three independent disk artifacts.
tasks.problemStatement: Given a filesystem event, application database event, and system event, determine whether they support a common sequence and state the limitations.
requirements: A supplied training CSV or forensic image; spreadsheet or Python.
tasks.hint: Do not use the closest timestamps alone; compare artifact semantics and source reliability.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The solution separates observations from interpretation and avoids unsupported attribution.

modules.title: Advanced Storage, Encryption, and Anti-Forensics
modules.description: Handle difficult cases involving encryption, SSD behavior, anti-forensics, RAID, and virtualized storage without overstating conclusions.

lessons.title: Full-Disk Encryption and Forensic Constraints
lessons.description: Explains how full-disk, volume, and file/folder encryption change acquisition and examination strategy.
learningObjectives: distinguish disk, volume, and file-level encryption
explain why a powered-off encrypted disk can be difficult to examine
identify lawful sources of keys or decrypted data in a case plan

notes.text: NIST SP 800-111 distinguishes full-disk, volume/virtual-disk, and file/folder encryption. SWGDE notes that encryption can require live acquisition to preserve access to decrypted data or keys. Possible key sources include recovery material, enterprise management systems, paired devices, or other authorized sources; the exact approach depends on the case and legal authority.
Do not teach or use unauthorized key extraction against third-party systems. In a forensic case, acquisition and decryption must be authorized and documented.

quiz.question: Why can live acquisition be important on an encrypted system?
options: It may preserve access to data or keys that become unavailable after shutdown.
It guarantees a complete image without side effects.
It proves who used the system.
quiz.answer: It may preserve access to data or keys that become unavailable after shutdown.
quiz.explanation: SWGDE explicitly notes live acquisition can be the only opportunity to obtain data from an encrypted system in some situations.

summary: Encryption can change the order and method of acquisition because shutting down a live system may remove access to decrypted data or keys.

resources.title: NIST SP 800-111 — Guide to Storage Encryption Technologies for End User Devices
SWGDE 17-F-002-2.1 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Acquisition

lessons.title: SSD, TRIM, and the Limits of Deleted-Data Recovery
lessons.description: Explains why flash storage can reduce the reliability of traditional deleted-file recovery and why acquisition timing matters.
learningObjectives: explain the purpose of TRIM at a high level
describe why SSD garbage collection can change remnants
avoid promising recovery of deleted SSD data

notes.text: TRIM allows an operating system to inform storage that blocks associated with deleted data are no longer needed. SSD controllers may also perform garbage collection and internal data movement. As a result, sectors that once held deleted data may no longer contain recoverable remnants when the examiner acquires the device.

items: TRIM behavior depends on the operating system, filesystem, controller, and device state.
A forensic image cannot recover bytes that were already discarded or overwritten before acquisition.
Absence of recovered data is not proof that the data never existed.

quiz.question: What is one reason SSD deleted-data recovery can fail?
options: TRIM and controller garbage collection can remove or alter remnants.
MFT records cannot exist on SSDs.
quiz.answer: TRIM and controller garbage collection can remove or alter remnants.
quiz.explanation: Flash storage can make previously recoverable blocks unavailable through TRIM and controller behavior.

summary: Traditional magnetic-disk recovery assumptions do not transfer cleanly to SSDs because controller behavior can remove or relocate remnants.

resources.title: SWGDE 17-F-002-2.1 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Acquisition

lessons.title: Anti-Forensics and Destructive Artifacts
lessons.description: Introduces wiping, timestamp manipulation, file hiding, encryption, and log clearing as hypotheses to investigate rather than labels to apply casually.
learningObjectives: identify common anti-forensic categories
recognize evidence that can suggest deliberate concealment
distinguish suspicious inconsistency from proof of anti-forensic intent

notes.text: Anti-forensic activity may include secure deletion/wiping, timestamp manipulation, concealment, encryption, log clearing, or deliberate corruption. SWGDE advises considering destructive activity and encryption during collection planning. A forensic examiner should document observable anomalies and seek corroborating evidence rather than declaring “anti-forensics” solely because an artifact is missing.

items: Look for inconsistencies across independent timestamps and metadata.
Examine filesystem journals and historical sources when available.
Document tool limitations and retention gaps before inferring deliberate deletion.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to report a suspected anti-forensic action?
options: Describe the observed anomaly, supporting artifacts, and limitations.
State that the suspect definitely wiped the disk.
Treat every missing file as evidence of wiping.
quiz.answer: Describe the observed anomaly, supporting artifacts, and limitations.
quiz.explanation: Forensic reporting should distinguish observations from conclusions and alternative explanations.

summary: Anti-forensics is best handled as an evidence-based hypothesis supported by multiple artifacts and known technical behavior.

resources.title: SWGDE 18-F-002-2.0 — Best Practices for Digital Evidence Collection
SWGDE 18-F-001-2.0 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Examinations

lessons.title: RAID, Virtual Disks, and Complex Storage
lessons.description: Introduces the additional reconstruction issues created by RAID, virtual machine disks, snapshots, and storage abstraction layers.
learningObjectives: identify why RAID can require multiple source devices
explain how virtual disks add a translation layer
plan evidence collection so metadata and configuration are preserved

notes.text: Complex storage can separate logical data from the physical devices an examiner initially sees. RAID may require multiple member devices and controller/configuration metadata. Virtual disks can contain partition tables and filesystems inside another host filesystem or storage container. Snapshots and thin provisioning can create additional layers that must be documented.
Do not reconstruct an unknown RAID or virtual-storage layout by trial and error on original media. Work from verified copies and preserve configuration metadata.

quiz.question: Why is RAID configuration metadata important?
options: It can be required to reconstruct the logical storage view from member devices.
It contains the user’s password by definition.
It makes a disk image unnecessary.
quiz.answer: It can be required to reconstruct the logical storage view from member devices.
quiz.explanation: Without layout information, the logical byte sequence may not be reconstructable from individual members.

summary: Complex storage requires layer-by-layer reconstruction and careful preservation of controller, hypervisor, and snapshot metadata.

tasks.title: Assess a Difficult Recovery Scenario
tasks.description: Write an acquisition and analysis plan for an encrypted SSD with possible deleted evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: The system is powered on, storage is encrypted, and the investigation concerns a file deleted recently. Produce a plan that balances volatile/decrypted evidence with later disk examination.
requirements: SWGDE acquisition guidance; NIST SP 800-111; a written scenario.
tasks.hint: Consider what becomes unavailable after shutdown and what evidence the SSD controller may already have discarded.
tasks.solutionCode:
Plan:
1. Confirm authority and scope.
2. Document live state and connected media.
3. Consider live collection of volatile/decrypted data and authorized encryption keys before shutdown.
4. Acquire storage using an approved, documented method with source protection.
5. Hash and verify the acquisition.
6. Examine current and historical filesystem artifacts.
7. Attempt deleted-file recovery while explicitly documenting SSD/TRIM limitations.
8. Correlate with host/application artifacts.
9. Report both positive findings and meaningful non-findings.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The plan reflects SWGDE guidance on live acquisition and encryption and acknowledges that SSD/TRIM behavior can make deleted-data recovery incomplete or impossible.

modules.title: Validation, Reporting, and Quality Assurance
modules.description: Turn technical examination into reproducible, reviewable findings through validation, reporting, and evidence packaging.

lessons.title: Tool Validation and Cross-Checking
lessons.description: Teaches how to validate forensic tools and important results through known test images, alternate tools, and low-level inspection.
learningObjectives: explain why forensic tools should be validated
design a simple known-answer test
cross-check an important result with an independent method

notes.text: SWGDE recommends selecting tools with known limitations and validating them according to organizational policy. Validation is not the same as trusting a brand name; it means demonstrating that the tool performs the function required for the case on representative data.

items: Define the function being tested.
Use a known test image with known expected results.
Run the tool and compare the output.
Record version, configuration, input, expected result, actual result, and deviations.
Re-test after significant version or configuration changes.

quiz.question: What is a known-answer test?
options: A test dataset with a predetermined expected result used to evaluate a tool.
quiz.answer: A test dataset with a predetermined expected result used to evaluate a tool.
quiz.explanation: Known-answer testing compares tool behavior against a controlled expected result.

summary: Tool validation makes results more defensible and exposes parser limitations before they affect a real investigation.

resources.title: SWGDE 17-F-002-2.1 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Acquisition

lessons.title: Forensic Reporting: From Artifact to Finding
lessons.description: Shows how to convert technical observations into clear, reproducible findings without overstating certainty.
learningObjectives: write findings that separate observation, interpretation, and conclusion
cite evidence locations and hashes
document methods, limitations, and alternative explanations

notes.text: A useful forensic report lets another examiner understand what was examined, how it was examined, what was observed, and why the stated conclusion follows. Findings should identify evidence identifiers, artifact locations, relevant timestamps, extraction methods, hashes of exported items when appropriate, and limitations.

items: Use precise artifact names and paths.
State whether a timestamp is filesystem, application, or system-log derived.
Do not infer identity or intent beyond what the evidence supports.
Record negative findings carefully when absence is meaningful and the search method was sufficient.

quiz.question: What should a strong finding include?
options: Observed evidence, interpretation, conclusion, and relevant limitations.
Only a screenshot with no context.
quiz.answer: Observed evidence, interpretation, conclusion, and relevant limitations.
quiz.explanation: The reader needs enough context to understand how the conclusion follows from the evidence and where uncertainty remains.

summary: A defensible report is reproducible, evidence-linked, and explicit about uncertainty.

resources.title: SWGDE 18-F-001-2.0 — Best Practices for Computer Forensic Examinations

lessons.title: Case Review, Peer Verification, and Quality Control
lessons.description: Introduces a structured review pass that checks hashes, source paths, tool outputs, timeline assumptions, and report wording before release.
learningObjectives: perform a technical peer-review checklist
identify common report inconsistencies
verify that exported evidence can be traced back to the image

items: Recalculate or verify image hashes.
Confirm evidence identifiers match the report.
Re-run critical commands where feasible.
Trace each major finding to its source artifact.
Check timestamps and timezone labels.
Review screenshots/exports for context and integrity.
Check that limitations are stated.
Ensure no analysis output overwrote evidence.

practicals.title: Perform a case quality-control review
practicals.description: Review a supplied mini-case report and evidence manifest for consistency.
steps: Compare the evidence manifest with report identifiers.
Recalculate the provided hash values where files are available.
Check one timeline entry against its source artifact.
Flag any claim that lacks an evidence reference or overstates certainty.
practicals.solution: Produce a review table with columns: issue, evidence reference, severity, correction, reviewer note.
practicals.output: The completed review identifies traceability or wording defects and proposes concrete corrections.

tasks.solutionCode:
Original claim: "The user deleted confidential.docx at 14:32."
Rewritten finding: "The NTFS metadata for confidential.docx records a deletion-related filesystem state at 14:32 as interpreted by the examination tool. This observation alone does not establish which person performed the action or the reason for it. Additional corroboration would be required for attribution."

project.name: Authorized Disk Image Examination and Evidence Report
project.description: A realistic capstone in which the student receives an authorized training disk image, preserves and verifies it, reconstructs the partition/filesystem layout, performs targeted filesystem analysis, extracts selected evidence, correlates artifacts into a timeline, and produces a concise evidence-linked report. The project is deliberately read-only and uses synthetic or legally obtained training data.
steps: 1. Define the investigative question, scope, and evidence identifier.
2. Preserve the supplied image and calculate a SHA-256 digest before analysis.
3. Record tool versions and create a case output directory separate from the evidence image.
4. Run mmls and manually review the partition layout; record the chosen partition offset.
5. Use fls to locate relevant files and metadata addresses.
6. Use istat to inspect the metadata for at least two relevant objects.
7. Extract one authorized target object with icat and hash the derived copy.
8. Examine available deleted-file or historical artifacts and state recovery limitations.
9. Build a timeline from at least three independent artifact observations.
10. Cross-check one major finding with a second method or lower-level view.
11. Write a report containing observations, interpretations, conclusions, evidence references, hashes, and limitations.
12. Generate a manifest of derived results and verify the final case package.
project.code:
# Disk Forensics Case Assistant
# Purpose: create a reproducible, read-only examination record for an authorized
# training image using The Sleuth Kit and standard hashing tools.
# This script does not modify the evidence image.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

IMAGE=${1:?Usage: $0 <image.raw> [output_dir]}
OUT=${2:-case-output}
mkdir -p "$OUT"

command -v sha256sum >/dev/null || { echo "sha256sum is required" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v mmls >/dev/null || { echo "mmls (The Sleuth Kit) is required" >&2; exit 1; }
command -v fls >/dev/null || { echo "fls (The Sleuth Kit) is required" >&2; exit 1; }

if [ ! -f "$IMAGE" ]; then
  echo "Evidence image not found: $IMAGE" >&2
  exit 1
fi

{
  echo "case_started_utc=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)"
  echo "image=$IMAGE"
  echo "sha256=$(sha256sum "$IMAGE" | awk '{print $1}')"
  echo "mmls_version=$(mmls -V 2>&1 || true)"
  echo "fls_version=$(fls -V 2>&1 || true)"
} > "$OUT/case-manifest.txt"

# Partition discovery. Review this output manually; do not assume an offset.
mmls "$IMAGE" > "$OUT/partition-layout.txt"

# The examiner supplies the verified partition offset from the reviewed mmls output.
OFFSET=${OFFSET:?Set OFFSET to the partition start sector after reviewing partition-layout.txt}

# File listing is read-only against the image.
fls -r -o "$OFFSET" "$IMAGE" > "$OUT/filesystem-list.txt"

# Optional targeted metadata extraction: supply an inode discovered from fls.
if [ -n "${INODE:-}" ]; then
  istat -o "$OFFSET" "$IMAGE" "$INODE" > "$OUT/target-istat.txt"
  icat -o "$OFFSET" "$IMAGE" "$INODE" > "$OUT/target-extracted.bin"
  sha256sum "$OUT/target-extracted.bin" > "$OUT/target-extracted.sha256"
fi

# Hash every derived result for the evidence manifest.
find "$OUT" -maxdepth 1 -type f ! -name '*-sha256.txt' -print0 | sort -z | xargs -0 sha256sum > "$OUT/results-sha256.txt"

echo "Examination outputs written to $OUT"
project.explanation: Architecture: the supplied disk image is immutable evidence; the Bash case assistant reads it through The Sleuth Kit and writes all outputs to a separate case directory. Data flow: image → SHA-256 manifest → mmls partition layout → examiner-selected partition offset → fls filesystem listing → istat metadata review → optional icat extraction → hashes of derived evidence → report/timeline. The examiner, not the script, makes the critical partition-offset and relevance decisions. This prevents automation from silently interpreting an incorrect offset. The script also refuses to run until required tools are present and requires OFFSET to be explicitly supplied after manual review. The final report should distinguish direct observations from interpretations and should document any inability to recover deleted data, encryption limitations, SSD/TRIM limitations, or parser uncertainty.
